summary: This experimental RFC defines a NETCONF capability for time-triggered operations. Clients can schedule configuration and management operations to happen at specific times, and servers can attach timestamps to the data they send.

plainLanguage.summary: You can tell a device to change its settings at a certain time, like setting an alarm clock, and the device can stamp its answers with the time.

questions: how does netconf time capability work
when should i use scheduled netconf commands
can i coordinate configuration changes across multiple devices
subtitle: Schedule configuration changes to happen at specific times.

tldr.problem: NETCONF clients cannot control when their Remote Procedure Call (RPC) commands execute on servers, making it hard to coordinate synchronized configuration changes across multiple devices.
tldr.mechanism: The time capability adds scheduled-time and get-time elements to NETCONF RPCs. A client can specify the time an RPC should execute, and can request the server to report the actual execution time.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can send identical configuration updates to many devices with the same scheduled time, ensuring they all change at nearly the same moment.

today: RFC 7758 is an experimental RFC. It is not yet part of the NETCONF standard, but is available for implementation and testing to gather feedback before potential future standardization.

sections.title: The Need for Time in NETCONF
sections.content:
NETCONF (RFC 6241) is the standard protocol for configuring network devices. Clients send Remote Procedure Call (RPC) commands to servers, which execute them immediately. The original protocol gives clients no control over the timing of execution and no feedback about when the RPC actually ran.

In many real-world scenarios, an operator needs to make the same configuration change to multiple devices at nearly the same time. For example, rolling out a software patch, switching traffic to a backup network, or collecting statistics at a synchronized moment. Without time control, the client must send each RPC sequentially, meaning each device receives the change at a slightly different time. This can create inconsistencies or race conditions.

This specification defines the :time capability, an experimental NETCONF extension that allows clients to schedule RPCs and to request execution timestamps. With scheduled execution, all devices can perform their configuration changes at the same time (within network propagation latency), and with timestamp reporting, clients can verify when each device actually executed the command.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF is how you tell network devices what to do. Before, you could only tell them "do this now." Now you can say "do this at 3:00 PM" and multiple devices will do it at the same time.

sections.title: How Time-Based Scheduling Works
sections.content:
The time capability provides two primary functions, both illustrated in Section 3.1 of the RFC:

Scheduling: When a client sends an RPC to a server, the message may include a scheduled-time element specifying the time at which the RPC should execute. The server stores the RPC and executes it at the designated time, then sends the RPC reply. This allows a client to send configuration updates to multiple servers with the same scheduled execution time, achieving coordinated changes.

Reporting: When a client sends an RPC, it may include a get-time element requesting that the server report back the execution time. After the server executes the RPC, it includes the actual execution time (Te) in the RPC reply. This allows the client to verify that the server executed the command when expected and to gather timestamped snapshots of system state across multiple servers.

A third scenario combines both: the client specifies both a scheduled time and requests time reporting, allowing coordinated execution with verification.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can say "execute this at time T" and also say "tell me when you actually did it." Many clients can send the same command with the same time, so all servers change together.

sections.title: Capabilities and Interactions
sections.content:
The time capability is implemented as a NETCONF capability identifier, as described in RFC 6241. A server that supports the :time capability advertises it in its NETCONF hello message, allowing clients to discover whether the server can handle scheduled RPCs and time reporting.

The time capability extends existing NETCONF operations. When a client sends an RPC, it can optionally add scheduled-time and/or get-time elements to any RPC that the server recognizes. Servers must be prepared to receive standard RPCs without these elements and to process them normally, maintaining backward compatibility with clients that do not use the time capability.

The specification defines the format for scheduled times (Section 3.4) and time intervals (Section 3.7), along with scheduling tolerance (Section 3.5) to allow for network delays and processing variations. It is intended for near-future scheduling (seconds to minutes), not for far-future scheduling or policies based on time-of-day.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tells the client: "I can handle scheduled commands." Then the client can include a time in its commands, and the server will wait until that time to execute them.

sections.title: Use Cases and Examples
sections.content:
Example 1 (Section 5.1): A network operator needs to commit a configuration change on 5 servers simultaneously. Without the time capability, the operator sends 5 commit RPCs in sequence; each server commits at a different moment. With the time capability, the operator sends 5 commit RPCs, each with scheduled-time set to 5 seconds in the future. All servers execute the commit at nearly the same time.

Example 2 (Section 5.2): A monitoring application collects statistics from multiple servers and needs a synchronized snapshot. Without the time capability, each get-config RPC returns data collected at a slightly different time. With the time capability, the client sends get-config RPCs with the same scheduled-time and includes get-time to receive the execution timestamp. All servers collect their data at the same moment, and the client knows exactly when each sample was taken.

Section 5.3 shows error handling: if a server cannot schedule an RPC at the requested time (for example, the time is in the past), it returns an error message.
sections.plainLanguage: One use: "all commit at 3:00 PM." Another use: "all take a snapshot at 3:00 PM and tell me what time you took it." If the time is wrong, the server says "that time already passed."
